feedback: If a child calls an edge a 'side' or a vertex a 'corner' and runs the properties together, pause and name each property against the object as they touch it: 'This flat part is a face; this straight line where two faces meet is an edge; this point where edges meet is a vertex.'
If the recount from a different starting face gives a different total, the marking slipped — re-mark systematically so each feature is counted exactly once.
If a child reaches only 3 faces or 9 edges, prompt: 'Turn the cube over — are there features round the back you haven't marked yet?'
activities.intendedInsight: A face, an edge and a vertex are three different things; counting each property separately in a fixed order, and marking features as you go, keeps them distinct and makes sure nothing hidden is missed or double-counted.
learnerActions: Hold a real cube and turn it in your hands.
Count the faces first: colour or number each flat surface as you touch it, saying 'face' each time, until every face is marked. Record the total.
Then trace each edge with a finger, marking each traced edge (e.g. a gold line or sticker), saying 'edge' each time, until all are traced. Record the total.
Then dot each vertex (corner) with a sticker, saying 'vertex' each time. Record the total.
Recount starting from a different face to check your totals stay the same (6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices).
activities.title: Count a real cube by touch in a fixed order

feedback: A child who predicts around 9 edges (the most you can see at once, when three faces are showing) is reasoning only about the visible faces — celebrate noticing the gap when the far-side edges bring the total to 12. (The '9' is a rough illustrative expectation, not a measured value; from one view you see at most 3 faces, 9 edges and 7 vertices.)

If a child reads all the information straight from the flat picture, prompt them to turn the real solid to check for features the picture hides; the point is linking the 2-D view to the full 3-D object.
If a friend's claim is used ('a cube has 3 faces because they can only see 3'), ask the child to explain, turning the cube, why that friend missed some.
Reinforce that recounting from a different face should reach the same total once hidden features are included.
activities.intendedInsight: A solid has features on its hidden far side that a flat picture does not show directly; a count based only on what you can see is too small, so you must turn the real object to catch every feature.
learnerActions: Before counting, look at a cube and predict out loud how many edges it has altogether, saying your number first.
Look at a flat picture or drawing of the cube next to the real cube, and point out which edges, faces and corners in the picture are hidden from view.
Now trace and mark every edge on the real cube together, turning it so the far side comes into view and you find the hidden features from the picture.
Compare your prediction with the counted total of 12, and talk about the edges 'round the back' you could not see at first.
Repeat the routine for vertices and faces: each time, predict the visible-only number aloud first, then turn the real solid to reach the full totals (8 vertices, 6 faces).
activities.title: Predict then count the hidden features

feedback: If a child says a cylinder has 3 faces, have them feel the round wall and ask whether it is flat like a face — then introduce 'curved surface' for it.
State explicitly which convention you are using, because schemes differ in how they describe curved solids; tell the child the rule you are following so they are not confused by other wording.
Reinforce by linking each flat face to the 2-D shape it matches (the circular faces of the cylinder, the square faces of the cube).
activities.intendedInsight: Under the convention used here, a face is a flat surface and an edge is a straight line where two flat faces meet; the round part of a cylinder or cone is described as a curved surface, not a face, and its curved boundary is not counted as an edge, while a cone has a pointed apex that many schemes call a vertex even though no edges meet there.
learnerActions: Hold a cylinder and run a hand over the round wall and over the flat ends.
Count the flat faces — the two circles on a cylinder — and mark them.
Decide whether the round wall is a face: feel that it is not flat, and name it a 'curved surface' rather than a face.
Check the circle-to-curve boundary: is it a straight line where two flat faces meet? Under the convention we are using, if not, it is not counted as an edge (some schemes call it a curved edge).
Say the full description: a cylinder has two flat (circular) faces and one curved surface.
Then repeat with a cone and note it has one flat circular face, one curved surface, and a single pointed apex; say whether your scheme calls the apex a vertex, since no edges meet there.
Compare the solids directly with the cube to contrast flat faces with a curved surface.
activities.title: Flat face versus curved surface

feedback: For a flat-faced solid, if the number of shapes in the net does not match the touch-count of faces, recount both and find the discrepancy together; for curved solids, expect one extra piece that forms the curved surface.
Emphasise that the whole solid is not the same as one of its flat faces — the solid is a 3-D object, each face is a flat 2-D shape.

Note for the adult: a paper or card net has a slight real thickness and is a physical model of the ideal flat faces, which mathematically have no thickness. Ask the child about the flat 2-D shape the card represents (a square, a circle), not whether the card itself can be held or how thick it is.
activities.intendedInsight: Each face of a 3-D solid is a 2-D shape; seeing the faces laid out flat in a net, each as its own shape, reinforces the face count and links 3-D solids to 2-D shapes.
learnerActions: For a solid you have counted (e.g. a cube), name the 2-D shape of each face (a square).
Unfold a net that folds up into the solid, laying out each face as a separate flat shape.

For a solid with only flat faces (e.g. a cube), count the flat shapes in the net and check the number matches the face count you found by touch; for a cylinder or cone, notice that one piece of the net becomes the curved surface, not a face.
Fold the net back into the solid to see each flat shape become a face.
Talk about the shape each face represents — a square, a circle — rather than about the card itself.
activities.title: Faces as 2-D shapes and nets

feedback: Recall questions check the totals but do not by themselves build the counting strategy — if a count is wrong, return to handling and marking the real solid rather than just stating the right number.
A child who can give numbers but cannot say how a face differs from an edge may be reciting; probe the distinction and reteach by touch if needed.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to state the counts and articulate the difference between the three properties shows the properties are genuinely held apart, not just recited.
learnerActions: Answer direct questions such as 'How many edges does a cube have?' and match a solid to its face count.
Explain in your own words what makes a face different from an edge, and an edge different from a vertex.
Respond to a friend's wrong claim (e.g. 'a cube has 3 faces because I can only see 3') by explaining and demonstrating the correct count.
activities.title: Check and explain the counts
